extracted.intended_audience: federal court judges and litigators handling news-misappropriation/media law disputes (defense counsel)
extracted.subtask_description: A defendant's appellate/bench brief arguing legal standards for when news may be rewritten or redistributed and why complainant (Associated Press) is not entitled to injunctive relief. It canvasses precedent, evidentiary sufficiency, equitable doctrines, and the distinction between facts and protected expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: News becomes public property when published
rubrics_metrics.description: When bulletins and early editions are published the news therein becomes public property and is available to the world at large for all purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because published news is public property, a court cannot prohibit defendant from rewriting and distributing news that has appeared in early editions of newspapers; publication puts an end to complainant's exclusive protection. (Discussed with citations to Davies v. Bowes, Nat'l Telegraph News Co. v. Western Union, Tribune Co. v. Associated Press.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Facts are not copyrightable; copyright protects form not facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright does not protect bare facts or 'mere annals'; it protects the author's composition or the form of statement, not the underlying facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities (e.g., Nat'l Telegraph News Co. v. Western Union; Tribune Co. cases; Bowker on Copyright) show that a mere recital of events is not the fruit of intellectual labor warranting monopoly; others may publish the same facts though not the exact expression except under fair use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection for gathered news is like trade secret until publication
rubrics_metrics.description: A gatherer of news or facts can have protection analogous to a trade secret while the information is kept confidential; that protection ends upon legitimate publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board of Trade v. Christie Grain & Stock Co. is cited: confidential communication under contract can delay 'publication' and retain protection until the gatherer gains its reward; once published, the product becomes public and usable by others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misappropriation requires taking before public dissemination
rubrics_metrics.description: Defendant may not lawfully publish news furnished by complainant if obtained before it was published by complainant's members; but using news after those members have published it is not misappropriation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: National Telegraph News Co. v. Western Union is limited to pre-publication appropriation; the brief argues that the cited case does not extend to use of news after it appears in published papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plaintiff lacks equitable standing where it engages in same conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Complainant cannot obtain equitable relief if it itself has engaged in the same practice it seeks to enjoin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If Associated Press regularly took 'tips' and used items from other papers (including defendant's), then it has been doing the same thing and is not entitled to equity; points to evidence of AP's long-standing custom of using news from other services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary sufficiency: 'information and belief' insufficient without particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavits stating facts 'on information and belief' without naming informants or showing actual use are inadequate to justify accusations of misappropriation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The brief criticizes affidavits (Stone, Hall) for failing to show actual use by defendant or to name informants, arguing such hearsay-style assertions don't establish the accused practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy of obtaining 'tips' — permissible unless via breach/confidentiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtaining 'tips' or information from published sources or rumors is legitimate so long as it is not procured by inducing breach of contract or violation of a confidential relation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kent Cooper's testimony is interpreted to mean the only limitation on obtaining rumors/tips is avoidance of inducing breaches of contract/confidential relations. The brief challenges vague distinctions between 'tips' and 'information'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between original investigation and re-use is legally irrelevant if plaintiff uses same methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Complainant's assertion that others must perform 'original investigation' before publishing the same news is of little weight if complainant itself uses information from other papers and 'tips' without independent investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The brief urges the court not to accept AP's fine distinction between learning a rumor and publishing without independent verification, since AP practices reveal similar reliance on published tips.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay or failure to complain undermines claim of wrongful practice (bad faith/laches inference)
rubrics_metrics.description: If complainant's employees observed alleged misconduct more than a year before suit and never informed their member or defendant, this delay suggests lack of good faith and weakens the claim for equitable relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The brief points to the delay (observations more than a year before suit) and asks why complainant didn't notify its member (New York American) or defendant earlier, implying the suit is precipitated by opportunistic motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ownership at common law limited to manuscript and first publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Literary property at common law is protected only to the extent of possession and use of the manuscript and its first publication; voluntary publication determines exclusive right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge Seaman's language in Tribune Co. v. Associated Press is invoked: voluntary publication fixes the scope of common law literary property, and once published, exclusive rights are not absolute.

rubrics_metrics.name: When product is public, others may dissect and use it to discover methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a gatherer makes the product public, third parties are entitled to use it and even dissect it to discover underlying methods or 'secrets'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if information had trade-secret-like protection while confidential, publication allows the world to make use of and analyze the published product; cited to Board of Trade reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish pre-publication wire-ticker/telegraph transmissions from published newspaper content
rubrics_metrics.description: The National Telegraph News Co. v. Western Union holding protects pre-publication transmissions (e.g., ticker/telegraph feeds) from appropriation before public release; it should not be extended to news after newspaper publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The brief concedes defendant may not lawfully publish news obtained before members' publication but insists the National Telegraph rule does not bar use of news once legitimately published in newspapers and sold to the public.
